problems.body: 1 kilogram = how many grams?

commonErrors.feedback: 100 is what a centi badge would mean. Kilo means ×1000: 1,000 grams.
10 is too small a jump. Kilo always means ×1000: 1,000 grams.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Kilo means ×1000 of the base unit.

hints: Applies to grams the same as any unit.
explanationVariants: Kilo means ×1000, so 1 kilogram is 1,000 grams.
Same badge, same rule: kilo always means a thousand.

problems.body: 1 meter = how many centimeters?

commonErrors.feedback: 1,000 belongs to a kilo or milli badge. Centi means 100 make a base unit: 100 centimeters.
10 is too few. It takes 100 centimeters to make one meter.

widget.fallbackFeedback: The centi badge means 100 of them make one base unit.

hints: The centi badge means 100 make one.
Applies to meters the same as any unit.
explanationVariants: 100 centimeters make 1 meter.
The centi badge: 100 small units per base unit.

problems.body: 500 centimeters = how many meters?

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies instead of divides. Going from cm (smaller) to m (bigger) means dividing: 500÷100=5.
50 divides by 10, but the centi badge needs ÷100. 500÷100=5.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Divide by 100 to turn centimeters into meters.

explanationVariants: 100 cm make 1 m, so 500 cm is 5 m.

problems.body: 4 kilometers = how many meters?

commonErrors.feedback: 400 applies only part of the badge. 1 km is 1,000 m, so 4 km is 4×1,000=4,000.
40 is far too small. 1 km is 1,000 m, so 4 km is 4,000 m.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply the kilometers by 1,000.

explanationVariants: 1 km is 1,000 m, so 4 km is 4,000 m.

problems.body: 7 kilograms = how many grams?

commonErrors.feedback: 700 applies only part of the badge. Kilo means ×1000: 7×1,000=7,000.
That skips the badge entirely. 7 kg is 7×1,000=7,000 g.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply the kilograms by 1,000.

explanationVariants: The kilo badge applies to mass the same as length.

problems.body: 9,000 milliliters = how many liters?

commonErrors.feedback: That multiplies instead of divides. Going from mL (smaller) to L (bigger) means dividing: 9,000÷1,000=9.
90 divides by 100, but the badge needs ÷1,000. 9,000÷1,000=9.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Divide the milliliters by 1,000.

explanationVariants: 1,000 mL make 1 L, so 9,000 mL is 9 L.

problems.body: A rectangle is 9 units by 7 units. What is its area?

commonErrors.feedback: 16 adds the sides instead of multiplying. Area is length×width: 9×7=63.
32 doubles the sum of the sides — that's perimeter's idea. Area multiplies: 9×7=63.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply the length by the width.

explanationVariants: 9×7=63 square units.
Area multiplies the two dimensions.

problems.body: A rectangle is 14 units by 6 units. What is its area?

commonErrors.feedback: 20 adds the sides instead of multiplying. Area is length×width: 14×6=84.
40 doubles the sum of the sides — that's perimeter's idea. Area multiplies: 14×6=84.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Multiply the length by the width.

explanationVariants: 14×6=84 square units.

problems.body: A rectangle is 8 units by 5 units. What is its perimeter?

commonErrors.feedback: 40 multiplies the sides — that finds AREA, not perimeter. Walking around: 2×(8+5)=26.
13 is only 8+5, halfway around. Double it for all four sides: 2×13=26.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the two sides, then multiply by 2.

explanationVariants: Add the sides, then double for all four.

problems.body: A rectangle is 11 units by 4 units. What is its perimeter?

commonErrors.feedback: 44 multiplies the sides — that finds AREA, not perimeter. Walking around: 2×(11+4)=30.
15 is only 11+4, halfway around. Double it for all four sides: 2×15=30.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the two sides, then multiply by 2.

explanationVariants: Add the sides, then double for all four.

problems.body: A wall is 12 feet wide and 9 feet tall. How many square feet need painting?

commonErrors.feedback: 42 finds the perimeter (2×(12+9)) — but painting covers the SURFACE, not the edge. Area: 12×9=108.
21 just adds the sides. Painting needs area: 12×9=108.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Painting covers a surface — that's area: length × width.

explanationVariants: Painting is area: 12×9=108.
The verb 'paint' signals area, not perimeter.

problems.body: A garden is 16 feet by 7 feet. How many feet of fencing surround it?

commonErrors.feedback: 112 finds the area (16×7) — but fencing traces the EDGE, not the surface. Perimeter: 2×(16+7)=46.
23 is only 16+7, halfway around. Double it: 2×23=46.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Fencing needs perimeter: add the sides, then double.

explanationVariants: Fencing is perimeter: 2×(16+7)=46.
The verb 'fence' signals perimeter, not area.

problems.body: What is half of a straight angle (180°)?

commonErrors.feedback: 180° is the WHOLE straight angle. Half of it is 180÷2=90°.
360° is DOUBLE a straight angle, not half. Half of 180 is 90.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Divide 180 by 2.

explanationVariants: 180÷2=90° — a right angle.
Half of a straight angle is a right angle.

problems.body: How many degrees are in a full turn?

commonErrors.feedback: 180° is a straight angle — half a turn. A full turn all the way around is 360°.
90° is a right angle — a quarter turn. A full turn is 360°.

widget.fallbackFeedback: A full turn all the way around is 360°.

hints: A full turn goes all the way around.
explanationVariants: A complete turn measures 360°.
360° is the benchmark for one full rotation.

problems.body: What is the angle from 12 o'clock to 5 o'clock?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 is the hour number, not the degree measure. Multiply by 30: 5×30=150.
30 is just one hour-jump. Five hours is 5×30=150.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count the hours (5), then multiply by 30.

explanationVariants: Five hour-jumps of 30° each.

problems.body: What is the angle from 12 o'clock to 6 o'clock?

commonErrors.feedback: 6 is the hour number, not the degree measure. Multiply by 30: 6×30=180.
90° would be 12 to 3. 12 to 6 is 6 hours: 6×30=180.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count the hours (6), then multiply by 30.

explanationVariants: 6×30=180°, a straight angle.
Halfway around the clock face is 180°.

problems.body: Is a 110° angle acute, right, or obtuse?

options.label: Acute
options.feedback: Acute means under 90°. 110 is well past that — obtuse.

options.label: Right
options.feedback: Right means exactly 90°. 110 is bigger than that — obtuse.

explanationVariants: 110° sits between 90° and 180° — obtuse.
Past the right-angle benchmark, short of straight.

problems.body: Is a 90° angle acute, right, or obtuse?

options.label: Acute
options.feedback: Acute means under 90°. 90 is not under — it's exactly at the benchmark: right.

options.label: Obtuse
options.feedback: Obtuse means over 90°. 90 is exactly at, not over — right.

hints: That's right, not acute or obtuse.
explanationVariants: Exactly 90° is always a right angle.
The exact benchmark, not approximate.

problems.body: A 25° angle sits next to a 65° angle, sharing a ray. What is the combined angle?

commonErrors.feedback: 40 subtracts the angles. Adjacent angles ADD: 25+65=90.
That multiplies the two angles — but combining side-by-side angles means adding: 25+65=90.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the two angle measures together.

explanationVariants: 25+65=90 — a right angle.
Adding the two adjacent measures.

problems.body: A 40° angle sits next to an 80° angle, sharing a ray. What is the combined angle?

commonErrors.feedback: 40 subtracts the angles. Adjacent angles ADD: 40+80=120.
That multiplies the two angles — but combining side-by-side angles means adding: 40+80=120.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the two angle measures together.

explanationVariants: Adding the two adjacent measures.

problems.body: Two angles sit on a straight line. One is 75°. What is the other?

commonErrors.feedback: 75 just repeats the known angle. The two must total 180°: 180−75=105.
15 subtracts from 90 instead of 180. Angles on a LINE total 180°: 180−75=105.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Subtract the known angle from 180.

explanationVariants: The line's two angles must total 180°.

problems.body: A right angle is split into two parts. One part is 28°. What is the other part?

commonErrors.feedback: 152 subtracts from 180 — but a RIGHT angle totals 90°, not 180. 90−28=62.
28 just repeats the known part. The two parts together total 90°: 90−28=62.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Subtract 28 from 90, not 180.

hints: A right angle's two parts total 90°.
explanationVariants: The two parts of a right angle must total 90°.

problems.body: Angles all the way around a point total 360°. Two known angles are 150° and 100°. What is the third?

commonErrors.feedback: 250 is just the sum of the two knowns (150+100) — not the missing angle yet. Subtract it from 360: 110.
210 subtracts from 180 instead of the full-turn total. Around a point is 360: 360−250=110.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the two known angles, then subtract from 360.

explanationVariants: Adding the knowns, then subtracting from 360.

problems.body: Four angles surround a point. Three are each 90°. What is the fourth?

commonErrors.feedback: 270 is just the sum of the three knowns (90+90+90). Subtract it from 360: 90.
That uses the straight-line total instead of the full-turn total. Around a point is 360: 360−270=90.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Add the three known angles, then subtract from 360.

explanationVariants: Three right angles leave exactly one more.

problems.body: An object's edge lands on the 7th tick mark on an eighths-ruler. As a fraction (over 8), what is the numerator?

commonErrors.feedback: 8 is the total ticks in a whole inch, not this measurement. The 7th tick is 7/8 — numerator 7.
1 would be the first tick. The 7th tick past 0 has numerator 7.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count the tick marks from 0.

explanationVariants: The 7th tick past 0 is 7/8.
Counting seven tick marks from 0 gives a numerator of 7.

problems.body: Simplify 6/8 to lowest terms. What is the denominator?

commonErrors.feedback: 8 is the denominator BEFORE simplifying. 6/8 shares a factor of 2 with 8 — dividing both gives 3/4, denominator 4.
3 is the simplified NUMERATOR, not the denominator. 6/8 simplifies to 3/4 — denominator 4.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Find the greatest common factor of 6 and 8, then divide both by it.

hints: Greatest common factor of 6 and 8 is 2.
explanationVariants: 6/8's greatest common factor is 2: gives 3/4.
Dividing both by 2 simplifies to 3/4.

problems.body: Five pencils measure 1/2, 1/2, 3/4, 5/8, and 1/2 inch. How many marks stack above the 1/2 tick?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 counts every pencil, not just the ones measuring 1/2. Only three pencils measured exactly 1/2: three marks.
1 undercounts — 1/2 appears more than once. Count every pencil at 1/2: three.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count how many times 1/2 appears in the list.

hints: Count occurrences of 1/2 in the list.
explanationVariants: 1/2 appears three times — three marks stack there.
Three pencils measured exactly 1/2.

problems.body: Using the same five pencils (1/2, 1/2, 3/4, 5/8, 1/2), how many measurements are on the plot in all?

commonErrors.feedback: 3 is only the tallest stack (at 1/2). Every measurement in the list counts: 5 total.
4 misses one measurement. There are 5 pencils listed in all.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count every measurement in the whole list.

hints: Count every pencil in the list.
explanationVariants: 5 pencils, 5 total measurements.
Every entry in the list counts once.

problems.body: A line plot shows button widths: 1/4 (×2), 3/8 (×1), 1/2 (×3), 5/8 (×1), 3/4 (×1). How many buttons measured MORE than 1/2 inch?

commonErrors.feedback: 5 includes the buttons at exactly 1/2 — but the question asks strictly MORE than 1/2. Only 5/8 and 3/4 qualify: 2.
8 counts every button on the whole plot. Only those past 1/2 qualify: 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Count only the stacks taller than the 1/2 tick.

hints: Look for stacks past the 1/2 mark.
explanationVariants: 5/8 and 3/4 are the only stacks past 1/2: 2 buttons.
Strictly more than 1/2 excludes the 1/2 stack itself.

problems.body: The longest button is 3/4 inch; the shortest is 1/4 inch. What is the difference, simplified? What is the denominator?

commonErrors.feedback: 4 is the denominator BEFORE simplifying (2/4). Simplified, that's 1/2 — denominator 2.
1 is the simplified NUMERATOR, not the denominator. 2/4 simplifies to 1/2 — denominator 2.

widget.fallbackFeedback: Subtract 1/4 from 3/4, then simplify.

hints: Simplify 2/4 using its greatest common factor.
explanationVariants: 3/4−1/4=2/4, simplifying to 1/2.
Subtracting like fractions, then simplifying the result.
